assessment:
This study addresses a critical limitation in deep brain imaging by developing and validating aberration-corrected microendoscopes based on long (6.4 mm and 8.8 mm) gradient index (GRIN) lenses. The authors aimed to extend previous aberration correction methods, which were limited to GRIN lenses shorter than 4.1 mm, to enable high-resolution two-photon calcium imaging in the most ventral regions of the mouse brain. The work combines optical simulations, 3D microprinting fabrication, synthetic calcium data analysis, and in vivo validation to demonstrate that corrected microendoscopes substantially improve imaging performance.

The key findings are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence. Ray-trace simulations predicted 3.35-3.50× increases in diffraction-limited FOV radius, which were validated experimentally with measured improvements of 1.53-2.17× in effective FOV radius (corresponding to 2.3-4.7× area enlargements). The authors transparently acknowledge that experimental improvements were somewhat lower than simulated predictions and provide plausible explanations including emission aberrations and experimental variability not captured in modeling. Importantly, the study goes beyond optical characterization to demonstrate functional advantages using synthetic calcium data, showing that corrected microendoscopes enable detection of more neurons with high SNR, reduce artificial correlations between adjacent neurons due to signal cross-contamination, and improve source demixing as quantified by GLM-based purity metrics. These computational findings are corroborated by in vivo experiments in mouse olfactory cortex, where corrected microendoscopes showed constant SNR across the FOV and no radial distance dependence of adjacent neuron correlations.

The methodological rigor is a major strength of this work. The optical design uses appropriate criteria (Maréchal criterion, Strehl ratio >0.8), the fabrication approach combines high-precision 3D microprinting with efficient molding for scalability, and the experimental validation employs multiple complementary approaches (subresolved films, fluorescent beads, brain slices, synthetic data, in vivo imaging). The synthetic calcium data analysis is particularly valuable, as it allows direct comparison with ground truth signals to quantify improvements in signal quality and source separation. Statistical analyses are appropriate throughout, using permutation tests for non-normal distributions and providing adequate sample sizes.

The study has some limitations that are appropriately acknowledged. The extended FOV is characterized by a curved focal plane, meaning cells at different radial positions are at different axial depths. The improvement for the 8.8 mm microendoscope was more modest than for the 6.4 mm version, and the correlation with ground truth signals showed only moderate improvement for the longer probe. Additionally, while the authors demonstrate proof-of-principle in mouse olfactory cortex, broader validation across different brain regions and species would strengthen confidence in generalizability. The comparison with alternative aberration correction methods (adaptive optics) is somewhat limited to literature citations rather than direct experimental comparison.

Overall, this work makes an important contribution to deep brain imaging technology by demonstrating that built-in aberration correction can be successfully applied to long GRIN lenses, providing a ready-to-use solution that requires no microscope modifications. The combination of enlarged FOV, improved spatial resolution, reduced signal cross-contamination, and minimal invasiveness represents a significant advance that will enable more precise investigation of neural population codes in deep brain structures. The findings will be of broad interest to neuroscientists studying ventral brain regions and the methodology could potentially be extended to imaging in larger mammals.
